definition: The process by which plants use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
The green pigment found in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
The organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place, containing chlorophyll.
A reactant in photosynthesis, absorbed by plants through stomata from the air.
The sugar produced during photosynthesis, used by the plant for respiration, storage and building materials.
A factor that is in short supply and therefore prevents the rate of photosynthesis from increasing further.
The amount of light available — increasing light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis up to a point.
The amount of CO₂ available — increasing CO₂ concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis up to a point.
A factor affecting the rate of photosynthesis — too high a temperature denatures enzymes and stops photosynthesis.
The relationship between light intensity and distance: light intensity is proportional to 1/distance². Doubling the distance quarters the light intensity.
An insoluble carbohydrate used for storage in plants, made from glucose produced in photosynthesis.
A carbohydrate made from glucose, used to build plant cell walls.
Fats and oils produced from glucose and used for storage in plants.
Mineral ions absorbed from the soil by plants, used along with glucose to make amino acids and proteins.
The process of releasing energy from glucose using oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water as waste products.
The process of releasing energy from glucose without oxygen, producing lactic acid in animals or ethanol and CO₂ in plants and yeast.
Adenosine triphosphate — the molecule used to transfer energy within cells for biological processes.
The organelle where aerobic respiration takes place, releasing energy from glucose.
The product of anaerobic respiration in animal cells and bacteria, causing muscle fatigue.
A product of anaerobic respiration in yeast and plant cells, along with carbon dioxide.
The anaerobic respiration of sugars by yeast, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide. Used in brewing and bread-making.
The amount of extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down the lactic acid that has built up during anaerobic respiration.
The sum of all chemical reactions occurring in the body, including both building up (anabolism) and breaking down (catabolism) reactions.
An insoluble carbohydrate used to store glucose in animal cells, particularly in the liver and muscles.
A waste product formed when excess amino acids are broken down in the liver — excreted in urine.
The number of breaths taken per minute — increases during exercise to supply more oxygen for aerobic respiration.
The number of times the heart beats per minute — increases during exercise to deliver more oxygen and glucose to muscles.
The tiredness and pain in muscles caused by the build-up of lactic acid during anaerobic respiration.
